entries.note: From French and Latin ars, which also meant practical skills or crafts; from a root meaning 'to fit together', and related to Latin [[arma]], because using weapons takes skill.
Built on [[art]] and not originally negative; Latin artificium meant a work of art or a skill, and an artifice is something made with skill.
German for art; künstlich ('artificial') comes from it, just as English [[artificial]] comes from [[art]], so AI is künstliche Intelligenz (KI) in German.
Came into English from French in the 14th century; it literally means 'made of hemp', which makes it related to [[cannabis]].
The same word as [[canvas]]: the idea is gathering opinions in a cloth bag, and the political sense is marked by spelling it with two s's.
Cotton duck, or duck canvas, is a tightly woven kind of canvas; this sense of duck comes from Dutch.
Began as non-adhesive strips of [[duck]] cloth called duck tape; the name moved to adhesive tape in WWII, and 'duct tape' is a folk etymology.
A white preparatory coating, borrowed from Italian for chalk or plaster, from Latin [[gypsum]] and ultimately Greek; it was traditionally made from rabbit-skin glue and chalk.
The painter was called 'the Greek' because he was a foreigner where he worked; he grew up in Venetian-ruled Crete and worked in Italy and Spain.
From the Dutch word for donkey, a thing that carries loads, much like a clothes horse; so an easel holding a canvas is a donkey carrying cannabis.
From Dutch schets, from Italian schizzo, and ultimately from Greek schedios, meaning temporary or made offhand, via an unattested Latin word.
From Dutch etsen, 'to cause to be eaten', so it is related to [[eat]]: etching eats away at a surface. It is unrelated to [[sketch]].
A Dutch word meaning 'landship', with the suffix of friendship; Henry Peacham spelled it landskip in 1606. A real landscape figuratively invokes a painting.
Taken from the end of [[landscape]] and reused in words like seascape and hellscape; the hosts discuss whether this counts as [[rebracketing]].
We call him by his first name; his surname van Rijn means 'of the river Rhine', and Harmenszoon is a patronymic meaning 'son of Harmen'.
'Da Vinci' only means 'of Vinci', so strictly he should be called Leonardo, the opposite of how we treat [[Rembrandt]].
Under Spanish naming he had two surnames; he chose to go by his mother's surname Picasso instead of his father's surname Ruiz.
The 1600–1750 style; the French word means irregular or bizarre, probably from Portuguese for an irregular pearl; later critics used it as an insult. Related to [[verruca]].
Goes back to the same Latin root as [[Baroque]], a word beginning with v; both share the idea of something warty, lumpy and irregular.
Caravaggio's dramatic lighting, in which figures emerge from a deep, dark background.
The artistic use of strong contrasts between light and dark to create volume and depth.
A lighter, playful late form of [[Baroque]]; it means shell work or rock work, from French rocaille with a playful repeated sound, so the word is partly made up.
Named by detractors; 'impressionists' appears in Louis Leroy's scathing 1874 review, and the name is thought to come from Monet's painting Impression, soleil levant.
A reaction to [[Impressionism]], which it saw as too focused on outward experience; it expressed inner experience through distorted forms and exaggerated colours.
A post-WWII movement that took [[Expressionism]] further, using abstraction to express spontaneous, uncensored action; the term became popular around the 1940s.
The origin of the name is uncertain: it may be a childish noise, or Ball and Huelsenbeck may have picked French dada ('hobby horse') at random from a dictionary.
Jess is surprised by Rob's British pronunciation 'yoo-RYE-nal'; Rob compares it with urinary and explains that stress shifts depending on the following syllables.
The signature on Duchamp's Fountain; Rob reads it as a pun on German Armut, 'poverty'.
Duchamp's female alter ego, a pun on the French phrase 'Éros, c'est la vie', 'sex is life'.
A 1930s back-formation from [[surrealism]], not its source; surreal means 'like something a surrealist would create'.
Coined around 1917 by Guillaume Apollinaire for a movement beyond [[realism]]; French sur means 'on top of', here in the sense of above or beyond.
One of several art techniques with fancy French names whose literal meanings are mundane; collage just means 'gluing'.
A French technique name that literally means 'chewed paper'.
A French technique name that literally just means 'cutouts'.
Named after Étienne de Silhouette, a frugal French controller-general of the 1750s; the reason is unclear: cheapness, his short term in office, or his own silhouette-making.
Not related to minimum or minuscule; from Latin miniare, 'to paint red', from [[minium]]. The meaning 'small' came from small manuscript illuminations and portrait miniatures.
From the same source as [[portray]], meaning to draw forth or trace out, related to Latin trahere; like [[landscape]], it named a type of painting first.
Mona is a contraction of [[Madonna]], 'my lady'; this is only the English name, since in Italian the painting is called [[La Gioconda]].
The Italian name of the [[Mona Lisa]], meaning 'the happy one' and punning on the sitter's name, Lisa del Giocondo.
French crayon first meant a chalk pencil and now means pencil; it comes from French craie, 'chalk', from Latin [[creta]].
Latin for chalk or pipe clay, of unknown root sense; it may be linked to Crete, or it may be a Celtic word for mud or clay.
Comes from Latin [[creta]], 'chalk'.
The Romans got their copper from Cyprus, but nobody knows whether copper is named after Cyprus or Cyprus after copper; the same puzzle as [[creta]] and Crete.
Painting with pigment in heated beeswax, used in ancient Greece, Egypt and Rome; it is the 'grandparent' of the modern [[crayon]].
Coined in 1903 by Alice Stead Binney from French craie, 'chalk', plus [[oleaginous]] ('oily'), after the paraffin wax in the crayons.
The rarest Crayola colour, sold 1997–98 before being renamed Scarlet; named for Paralympian Gary Woodring, with torch meaning the Olympic torch.
A yellow-orange Crayola colour retired in 2017 to make room for Bluetiful, inspired by YInMn Blue; it became a collector's item and returned in 2025.
Comes from porphyra, a valuable pigment that was traded as a symbol of wealth.
A Crayola colour that began as Flesh Tint (1903), was shortened to Flesh in 1949, was briefly Pink Beige, and became Peach in 1962.
A Crayola colour from 1949, renamed Midnight Blue in 1958 because Prussia was no longer relevant.
